key_factors: (b) essential character of the aluminum alloy sheet
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the aluminum alloy sheet in coils in China
flip: Importing aluminum ingots or unwrought slabs of heading 7601 into Canada to be rolled into sheets of heading 7606 there.
reasoning: The product is imported as rectangular aluminum alloy sheets (0.60 mm thick) notched at the corners, classified in heading 7606 (subheading 7606.12), not heading 9506. Under 19 CFR 102.20, heading 7606 requires a change from any other heading. The Chinese aluminum coils are also classified in heading 7606, so slitting, painting, cutting-to-size, and corner notching in Canada do not satisfy the tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3) (similar to N316637 and N316780). Under 102.11(b)(1), the Chinese aluminum sheet imparts the essential character, making China the country of origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 2208.50
decisive_step: Macerating neutral grain alcohol with juniper and botanicals and distilling into gin in Canada
flip: If imported bulk gin (2208.50) from the Netherlands were merely diluted with water and bottled in Canada without undergoing distillation there, the country of origin would be the Netherlands.
reasoning: The finished gin is classified in subheading 2208.50, HTSUS. The 192-proof neutral grain alcohol (96% ABV) from the Netherlands is classified in heading 2207 (undenatured ethyl alcohol of 80% ABV or higher), and the botanicals are classified in Chapter 9 or 12. In Canada, these foreign materials are macerated and redistilled into gin, undergoing the required tariff shift to subheading 2208.50 under 19 CFR 102.20(d). Therefore, pursuant to 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), the country of origin is Canada.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the aluminum wine rack pegs (or Canadian panels if the panels are made in Canada and shift)
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the aluminum wine bottle pegs in China (or fabrication of the panels in Canada)
flip: If the aluminum pegs were manufactured in Canada, or if the panels were determined to impart the essential character under GRI 3(b) and 102.11(b), the origin would be Canada.
reasoning: The kit is an unassembled composite wall-mounted wine rack (GRI 2(a), 3(b)). In Canada, the vinyl skin is applied to the acrylic panel and packaged with the MDF panel, aluminum pegs, and hardware. Merely packaging the unassembled kit components together in Canada does not result in a qualifying tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.17. Under 102.11(b)(1), the component that imparts the essential character to the wine rack (the Chinese aluminum pegs holding the wine bottles) determines the country of origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 8421.29
decisive_step: Drilling the casing and assembling/welding the mesh jacket, centralizer, and casing in Canada.
flip: If the 102.20 rule for 8421.29 prohibited a shift from subheading 8421.99, the Country A mesh jacket would fail to shift and origin would be Country A under 102.11(b).
reasoning: The finished proMESH sand control screen is classified in subheading 8421.29.00. Under 19 CFR 102.20(o), the tariff shift rule for 8421.11–8421.39 requires 'A change to subheading 8421.11 through 8421.39 from any other subheading, including another subheading within that group.' All foreign materials—the mesh jacket (8421.99.01), centralizer (Chapter 73), and L-80 casings (Chapter 78/73)—are classified outside subheading 8421.29 and undergo the required tariff shift via drilling and welding in Canada. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), the origin is Canada.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 2106.90
decisive_step: Blending and formulating the cane sugar, maple syrups, water, salt, and natural flavoring into pancake and waffle syrup in Canada
flip: If the final syrup were classified under heading 1702 (e.g., 1702.90 as a sugar syrup without added flavoring/coloring) rather than 2106.90, the foreign cane sugar (heading 1701) would fail the 102.20 tariff shift for heading 1702 ('from any other chapter') and confer its foreign country of origin under 102.11(b).
reasoning: The retail-packaged blended pancake and waffle syrup ('Maple Blend 3') contains added salt and natural flavoring, placing it in subheading 2106.90 as a food preparation not elsewhere specified. Under 19 CFR 102.20, subheading 2106.90 requires a shift from any other subheading with exceptions (such as dairy of Ch. 4 or juices of 2009) that do not apply here. Foreign ingredients (such as cane sugar of 1701, salt of 2501, or flavorings of 3302) shift to 2106.90 in Canada (consistent with N320159 and N326397). Origin is Canada under 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 1904.20
decisive_step: Mixing, blending, and manufacturing the cereal ingredients into the finished cereal product in Canada
flip: If the 13% U.S. cereal flakes were already unroasted flakes classified in subheading 1904.20, they would fail the tariff shift and confer United States origin under 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1).
reasoning: The finished cereal is a Musli-type preparation of unroasted oats, cereal flakes, nuts, seeds, and dried fruits classified in subheading 1904.20. The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for 1904.20 requires a change from any other subheading. All foreign ingredients—including roasted/puffed cereal flakes (1904.10), nuts/fruits (Ch. 8, 20), seeds (Ch. 12), inulin (1108), oils (Ch. 15), salt (2501), and flavors (2106/3302)—are classified outside 1904.20 and undergo the required tariff shift in Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 8541.43 from any other subheading, including 8541.42
decisive_step: Manufacturing and assembling the solar cells and other components into finished solar panels in Mexico
flip: Importing already-assembled solar panels/laminates classified in subheading 8541.43 into Mexico for minor framing or testing, which would fail the subheading shift.
reasoning: Under the 2024 HTSUS and Note 10 to Chapter 85, the finished solar panels are classified in subheading 8541.43, whereas unassembled photovoltaic cells are classified in subheading 8541.42. Unlike earlier precedent H266527 (when both cells and panels shared subheading 8541.40), the 102.20 rule for headings 8541-8542 allows a shift from any other subheading within heading 8541. Because foreign cells (8541.42) and other foreign components shift to 8541.43 in Mexico, Mexico is the country of origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 1605.52
decisive_step: Enrobing the frozen scallop medallions in raw bacon in Canada, shifting the scallops from Chapter 3 to Chapter 16.
flip: If the scallop medallions were pre-cooked or otherwise prepared in China so as to be classified in heading 1605 prior to import into Canada, they would fail the chapter shift and origin would be China under 102.11(b)(1).
reasoning: Following precedent N326450, frozen raw bacon-wrapped scallop medallions are classified in subheading 1605.52.6000 because the raw bacon comprises more than 20 percent by weight of the product (here 55 percent), placing it in Chapter 16 per Note 2 to Chapter 16. The Chinese frozen scallops (heading 0307) are foreign to Canada and undergo the required tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.20(c) from any other chapter to heading 1605 when wrapped in bacon in Canada. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), the origin is Canada.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift of all foreign materials to heading 3926
decisive_step: Perforating the LDPE sleeves and thermo-fusing the drip lines, sleeves, and film into the finished composite Irrigator Mantle Technology in Mexico.
flip: If the finished IMT were classified by essential character under GRI 3(b) in heading 3917 or 3920 rather than heading 3926, the corresponding foreign material would fail the tariff shift and origin would be determined under 102.11(b) or (c) as United States or Chile.
reasoning: The Irrigator Mantle Technology (IMT) is a composite good manufactured in Mexico by punching Chilean LDPE sleeves (heading 3917) and thermo-fusing them with U.S. perforated LDPE drip lines (heading 3917) and Chilean LDPE film (heading 3920). Because the fused article goes beyond mere tubes or flat film, it is classified in heading 3926 as other articles of plastics. Under 19 CFR 102.20, all foreign materials shift from headings 3917 and 3920 to heading 3926, conferring Mexican origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (b) essential character imparted by the South Korean Cover Casting and Main Board Casting
decisive_step: Casting and forming of the aluminum Cover Casting and Main Board Casting in South Korea
flip: Cast and form the Cover Casting and Main Board Casting in Mexico so all foreign materials undergo the required tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3).
reasoning: The adapter plate assembly is a specialized motor vehicle part classified under subheading 8708.99 (or alternatively a chiller part under 8418.99 / 8419.90). The steel fasteners (7318) shift to 8708.99, and the Mexican gasket is domestic. However, the South Korean Cover Casting and Main Board Casting are already dedicated vehicle parts of 8708.99 (or same part subheading) and fail the 102.20 shift. Under 19 CFR 102.11(b), the two South Korean castings impart the essential character, making the origin South Korea.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 3824.99
decisive_step: Blending the mineral oil, surfactant, xanthan gum, guar powder, and Bentone in Canada to form the chemical preparation
flip: If the CAS Premium Mineral Oil exceeded 60% by weight of the finished product, the 102.20 rule for 3824.99 would fail and origin would shift to the United States under 102.11(b)(1).
reasoning: Lubrigel L is a chemical preparation for oilfield drilling containing 50.75% mineral oil, 27% xanthan gum, and 18% guar powder, classified in subheading 3824.99 (as petroleum oil is under 70% by weight). Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) and 102.20, the rule for 3824.99 requires a shift from any other subheading, provided no single substance exceeds 60% by weight. All foreign ingredients shift from their respective headings (2710, 3402, 6806, 3913, 1302) and the largest component is 50.75%. Origin is Canada.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 7610 (and even under (b), the Canadian-extruded aluminum structural components impart the essential character)
decisive_step: Extrusion, cutting, welding, and fabrication of the Turkish aluminum billets and U.S. fabric into the freestanding aluminum canopy structure in Canada
flip: If the aluminum structural extrusions and components were already fabricated into parts of structures of heading 7610 in Turkey prior to importation into Canada for simple assembly.
reasoning: CBP rejected heading 6306 because the product is a permanently affixed freestanding aluminum structure, classifying it under heading 7610 (7610.90.0080). The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for heading 7610 requires a change from any other heading. In Canada, Turkish aluminum billets (heading 7601) are extruded (consistent with N325521 and N326606), cut, tapped, welded, and painted, and U.S. fabric is cut and sewn into the canopy. All foreign materials shift to heading 7610 under 102.11(a)(3), conferring Canadian origin.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the Indonesian plywood substrate (the only material that failed the tariff shift under 102.18(b))
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the 8mm-thick hevea plywood substrate in Indonesia
flip: Manufacturing the plywood substrate in Canada from veneers of heading 4408 so all foreign materials shift to heading 4412 under 102.11(a)(3).
reasoning: The finished multilayer wood flooring is classified in 4412.31. Under 19 CFR 102.20(h), goods of headings 4401-4421 require a change from any other heading. In Canada, the U.S. or Canadian face ply (heading 4407/4408) shifts to 4412, but the Indonesian plywood substrate (4412.31) remains in heading 4412 and fails the shift under 102.11(a)(3). Proceeding to 102.11(b)(1) and 102.18(b)(1), only the failing Indonesian plywood substrate is considered, imparting the essential character and making Indonesia the country of origin.

key_factors: (d)(3) last country where the good underwent production, as no single failing component (rack, pinion, housing, or ball joints) alone imparts the essential character under (b)
decisive_step: Final assembly of the Manual Rack and Pinion Gear (MRP) in Mexico from multi-country components.
flip: If a single foreign component (such as a pre-assembled rack-and-pinion housing subassembly from one country) imparted the essential character of the MRP, origin would be decided under 102.11(b) in that component's country (as in N301716).
reasoning: The Manual Rack and Pinion Gear (MRP) is classified in subheading 8708.94. Under 19 CFR 102.20, subheading 8708.94 requires a change from any other subheading. Because dedicated steering parts (rack gear, pinion gear, housing, IBJ, and OBJ) are also classified within subheading 8708.94 (8708.94.75), the foreign components fail the tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3). Under 102.11(b), no single component alone imparts the essential character of the complete rack-and-pinion system. Under 102.11(d)(3), origin is Mexico, where final production occurs.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the aluminum wine pegs
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the aluminum wine pegs in India
flip: If the aluminum wine pegs were extruded and machined in Canada, the origin would be Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(2) or (a)(3).
reasoning: Following directly on-point precedent N337479 (and N336902) for the 3-foot version of the same VINdustry wine peg and panel kit with identical component origins and value ratios, the unassembled composite good takes its classification and essential character from the aluminum pegs produced in India. Under 19 CFR 102.17, merely gathering kit parts and affixing a decorative vinyl skin in Canada does not qualify for a tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3). Under 102.11(b)(1), the Indian aluminum pegs impart the essential character, making the origin India.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 8483.40 (or (b) essential character of the gear races if no shift occurs)
decisive_step: Machining, heat treatment, tooth cutting, and assembly of the slew bearings in Mexico
flip: If the inner and outer races already have their gear teeth cut and are fully machined in China prior to assembly, or have a pre-determined end-use lacking substantial transformation in Mexico, origin would be China.
reasoning: Because the facts clearly state the slew bearings have gear teeth and are classified in heading 8483 (specifically 8483.40 as gears and gearing) rather than 8482 (distinguishing N318162), the 102.20 rule requires a shift to 8483.40 from any other subheading, including parts in 8483.90 (unless by GRI 2(a)). Processing and assembling the races (8483.90) with balls/rollers (8482.91) into finished geared slewing rings (8483.40) in Mexico satisfies 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 7326
decisive_step: Slitting, stamping, forming, and perforating the steel coils into bands and housings and assembling them with the screw into finished hose clamps in Canada
flip: If the bands and housings were pre-formed in India or China (classified in 7326) and merely assembled with the screw in Canada, the components of heading 7326 would fail to shift from another heading, shifting the analysis to 102.11(b).
reasoning: The finished stainless steel worm-drive hose clamps are classified under heading 7326 (7326.90.86). Under 19 CFR 102.20(n), the rule for heading 7325-7326 requires a change from any other heading, including another heading within that group. The flat-rolled stainless steel coils from India (heading 7220) and the screw from China (heading 7318) are processed and assembled in Canada into finished hose clamps of heading 7326. Because every foreign material satisfies the tariff shift in Canada, the origin is Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (b) for marking if restricted to the sole non-shifting foreign part (China), or (a)(3) / substantial transformation in Mexico where the PCBA, IU, DU, and TC are manufactured and assembled with the transport
decisive_step: Manufacture of the PCBA, imaging unit, developing unit, and toner cartridge in Mexico and their final integration with the printer transport in Mexico
flip: If the imaging unit, developing unit, and toner cartridge were manufactured in China and imported into Mexico as part of the printer transport (as in HQ H304677), the origin would be China.
reasoning: Distinguishing HQ H304677, where the Chinese printer transport included nearly all mechanical printing components and imparted the essential character, Lexmark shifted production of the imaging unit, developing unit, and toner cartridge to Mexico alongside the PCBA and firmware installation. Because the core image-forming and electronic control subassemblies (accounting for 61% of total manufacturing hours) are now manufactured and integrated in Mexico, the components undergo a substantial transformation in Mexico, making Mexico the country of origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 3923 (or (b) essential character of the pouch imparted by the polyethylene film if the spout is in 3923.50, though under 102.18(b) if only the Chinese spout fails, origin would be China unless the film is what fails or de minimis applies; however, cutting and heat-sealing film into a spouted pouch in Mexico shifts the film from 3920/3921 to 3923 and the spout from 3926/8481 to 3923)
decisive_step: Cutting and heat-sealing the polyethylene film into pouches and incorporating the spouts in Mexico
flip: If the pouches were already formed in China and only the spouts were attached in Mexico, both would be in heading 3923 and fail the tariff shift, making the origin China.
reasoning: The finished polyethylene pouch with spout is classified in heading 3923 (3923.21). The 102.20 rule for headings 3922-3926 requires a change from any other heading, including another heading within that group. In Mexico, the Chinese printed polyethylene film (heading 3920 or 3921) is cut and heat-sealed into pouches and combined with the Chinese plastic spout (heading 3926 or 8481, or de minimis if 3923.50). Because the foreign materials undergo the required tariff shift in Mexico, origin is Mexico under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (b) essential character imparted by the Chinese-origin forged valve blanks
decisive_step: Electric upsetting, extrusion, and heat treatment of bar stock into valve blanks in China
flip: Perform the electric upsetting and extrusion (forging of the raw steel bar stock of Chapter 72 into the rough shape of the valve blank) in Mexico so that the material shifts from Chapter 72 to heading 8409 in Mexico.
reasoning: The finished intake and exhaust valves for diesel engines are classified in subheading 8409.99. In China, raw steel bar is upset and extruded into the rough shape of a valve ('valve blank'), which already has the essential character of a finished valve under GRI 2(a) and is classified in heading 8409. Because the 102.20 rule requires a shift to 8409.91-8409.99 from any other heading, machining and plating in Mexico fail to shift tariff headings. Under 102.11(b)(1), the blanks impart the essential character, making China the country of origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 7610
decisive_step: Extrusion and fabrication (cutting, tapping, welding, powder coating) of Turkish aluminum billets into canopy framework components in Canada.
flip: If the aluminum profiles were already extruded and fabricated into structural parts of heading 7610 in Turkey and merely packaged in Canada, the country of origin would be Turkey.
reasoning: The complete aluminum canopy framework (imported unassembled without its fabric cover) is classified as an aluminum structure under heading 7610 (specifically subheading 7610.90). Under 19 CFR 102.20(n), the rule for heading 7610 requires a change from any other heading. Consistent with precedent N339969 (and extrusion rulings N325521 and N326606), the Turkish aluminum billets (heading 7601) are extruded, cut, tapped, welded, and powder-coated in Canada into structural framework components of heading 7610. Thus, the foreign materials satisfy 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), conferring Canadian origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 3206.11
decisive_step: Surface treatment, drying, and grinding of titanium dioxide into pigment in Canada
flip: If the titanium dioxide imported from China into Canada had already been surface-treated or prepared as a pigment of subheading 3206.11 prior to export from China, it would fail the tariff shift in Canada and origin would be China under 102.11(b)(1).
reasoning: The finished Titanium Dioxide Pigment is classified in subheading 3206.11.0000, HTSUS. The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for 3206.11 requires a change from any other subheading. In Canada, the Chinese intermediate Titanium Dioxide of heading 2823.00.0000 undergoes dispersion, chemical surface treatment, drying, and grinding to become a pigment of subheading 3206.11. Because all foreign inputs shift from outside subheading 3206.11 (consistent with the 3206 analysis in N334326), the country of origin is Canada pursuant to 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 8471.70
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the storage modules and assembly of the Serverless Rack in Mexico by BDT de México
flip: If the nine storage modules (8471.70) were imported into Mexico already assembled from China and merely mounted into the cabinet in Mexico, they would fail the tariff shift from any other subheading to 8471.70, flipping origin to China under 102.11(b).
reasoning: The Serverless Rack is a mass magnetic tape storage unit meeting Note 6(C) to Chapter 84, classified in subheading 8471.70 (unlike the server rack in NY N342790). The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for 8471.70 requires a shift from any other subheading except 8471.49. BDT de México manufactures the storage modules and integrates the rack in Mexico from foreign parts and subassemblies (8473.30 and other headings), satisfying the tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) and conferring Mexican origin.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the self-adhesive paper and polypropylene labelstock jumbo rolls
decisive_step: Coating, laminating, and manufacturing of the self-adhesive jumbo rolls in China
flip: Slitting the paper rolls in Canada or Mexico to a width not exceeding 15 cm (approx. 5.9 inches), or manufacturing the adhesive-coated jumbo rolls in Canada/Mexico from uncoated base paper/film of another heading.
reasoning: Following precedent N341007 (involving identical facts), the imported self-adhesive paper (4811.41) and polypropylene (3919.90) labelstock rolls measure 10 to 22 inches (25.4 to 55.88 cm) in width. Slitting jumbo rolls of Chinese origin into 10-22 inch rolls in a USMCA country does not satisfy the 19 CFR 102.20 tariff shift rules for headings 4811 (since widths exceed 15 cm) or 3919. Under 19 CFR 102.11(b), the Chinese jumbo rolls impart the essential character, making the origin China.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 8708.22 (or 7007.21)
decisive_step: Heating, bending, annealing, laminating the flat glass, and installing brackets, sensors, and pins in Mexico.
flip: If the glass were already bent, laminated, and framed into an unfinished windshield of 8708.22 (or 7007.21) in China prior to import into Mexico, it would fail the tariff shift and origin would be China.
reasoning: The finished automotive windshield with installed sensors, brackets, and pins is classified under subheading 8708.22 (or heading 7007 if considered unframed laminated safety glass). The Chinese flat glass is classified in heading 7005 or 7006. In Mexico, the flat glass is furnace-heated, press-bent, annealed, laminated, and fitted with sensors, brackets, and pins. Every foreign material shifts from its respective heading/subheading to 8708.22 (or 7007), satisfying 19 CFR 102.20 and conferring Mexican origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (b) essential character imparted by the single foreign material (the raw carbon steel forging from China, Italy, or India respectively)
decisive_step: Heating and forging the cut steel billet into a rough forging in the shape of the flange or fitting in China (or Italy or India, depending on where the forging was produced).
flip: Import raw steel billets of heading 7207 into Mexico and perform the forging into rough shapes and subsequent machining in Mexico, satisfying the tariff shift to heading 7307.
reasoning: Finished steel flanges and fittings are classified in heading 7307. The rough forgings imported into Mexico from China, Italy, or India already have the approximate shape of the finished goods and are classified in heading 7307 (either under subheading 7307.91.10/30 for unmachined flange forgings or via GRI 2(a)). Because machining in Mexico does not cause a shift from another heading as required by 19 CFR 102.20, 102.11(a)(3) fails. Under 102.11(b)(1), the single foreign forging imparts the essential character (China, Italy, or India).

key_factors: (b) essential character of the single material (nickel powder)
decisive_step: Hydrometallurgical manufacturing of the pure nickel powder in Australia
flip: If the Australian material were imported into Canada as unwrought nickel (heading 7502) and converted into powder in Canada, or if the powder were converted into nickel flakes in Canada, it would undergo the required tariff shift to confer Canadian origin under (a)(3).
reasoning: The finished good is pure nickel powder classified in 7504.00.00. It is not wholly obtained or produced exclusively from domestic materials in Canada under 102.11(a)(1)-(2). Under 102.11(a)(3), the 102.20 rule for heading 7504 requires a shift from another heading, or to flakes from powders of 7504. The Australian nickel powder enters Canada under 7504.00.00 and remains powder of 7504.00.00 after screening, cutting, and blending. Thus, it fails the tariff shift. Under 102.11(b)(1), the single material (Australian nickel powder) imparts the essential character, making Australia the country of origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift from heading 8714 to heading 8712
decisive_step: Assembly of the separate bicycle components into a 90% assembled bicycle in Canada
flip: If the foreign components were imported into Canada together as an unassembled bicycle kit classified in 8712 via GRI 2(a), or if simple assembly failed a specific subheading rule (unlike 8711 in H302204, 8712 allows a shift from 8714 through actual assembly), origin would be decided under 102.11(b) by the frame's origin (as in N295820).
reasoning: The complete bicycle is classified in heading 8712 (imported 90% assembled, having the essential character of a complete bicycle under GRI 2(a)). The 102.20(p) rule for 8712 requires a change from any other heading, except from 8714 pursuant to GRI 2(a). Because the foreign components from Taiwan, China, and Japan are imported separately into Canada as parts under heading 8714 and physically assembled into the bicycle in Canada (not merely collected as an unassembled GRI 2(a) kit), they make the tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 8708.99
decisive_step: Permanent assembly of the Taiwanese oil seal and Indian bearing cone under >1,000 ft-lbs of force in Mexico (or Taiwan/China in their respective scenarios)
flip: If the finished assembly were classified in heading 8482 ( specifically 8482.20), the Indian bearing cone (8482.20) would fail the tariff shift rule for 8482.10-8482.80, shifting origin to India under 102.11(b).
reasoning: Because the attached oil seal adds significant non-friction sealing and articulation functions for the wheel hub, the assembly is excluded from heading 8482 and classified as a motor vehicle part under subheading 8708.99. In the USMCA (Mexico) scenario, the Taiwanese oil seal (4016.93) and Indian bearing cone (8482.20) both shift from other headings to 8708.99 when permanently joined in Mexico, satisfying 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) and conferring Mexican origin.

key_factors: (d)(3) last country where the good underwent production, other than minor processing, as no single failing material imparts essential character under (b)
decisive_step: Manufacturing and production of the chair components and seat assembly in Mexico
flip: If all seat parts of 9401.99 were imported from China and merely underwent simple assembly or packaging in Mexico without Mexican production, origin would be China under (b) or (d)(2).
reasoning: The WP1000 Mesh Chair is classified in subheading 9401.39. The 102.20 rule for 9401.10-9401.80 requires a shift from any other subheading except 9401.90-9401.99. Foreign seat parts from China classified in heading 9401.99 fail the tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3). Under 102.11(b), no single failing component imparts the essential character to the complete chair. Consistent with precedents N319373, N335274, and N332384, analysis proceeds to 102.11(d)(3), conferring origin to Mexico as the last country where the good underwent production.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the single material (flat-rolled steel coil) that did not undergo the required tariff shift
decisive_step: Melting, pouring, rolling, galvanizing, and painting the steel coils in Brazil
flip: If the steel coils were manufactured in Mexico from slabs of heading 7207, or if the finished sheets were further prepared for use in structures so as to be classified in heading 7308, the origin would be Mexico.
reasoning: The roll-formed angular roofing sheets are classified in heading 7216 (specifically 7216.91) per EN 72.16. The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for heading 7216 requires a change from any other heading, except from headings 7208 through 7215. The Brazilian flat-rolled painted/galvanized coils are classified in heading 7210 or 7212, which are excluded from making the tariff shift. Under 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1), the single material that fails the shift (the Brazilian steel coil) imparts the essential character, making the origin Brazil.

key_factors: (a)(1) wholly obtained or produced in a single country
decisive_step: Collection of the semen from live stallions in Canada
flip: Collecting the semen from stallions in another country and merely packaging it into syringes in Canada.
reasoning: The horse semen is classified under subheading 0511.99.4025, HTSUS. Under 19 CFR 102.1(g)(4), products obtained from live animals in a country are a 'good wholly obtained or produced' in that country. Because the semen is collected from stallions in Canada and packed there for export, the good is wholly obtained or produced in a single country. Therefore, pursuant to 19 CFR 102.11(a)(1), the country of origin of the horse semen is Canada.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 8507.90
decisive_step: Forming the steel into the cylindrical battery can and assembling with the rivet and gasket in Mexico
flip: If the cylindrical can body were already formed in South Korea (classified in 8507.90) and merely assembled with the rivet and gasket in Mexico, it would fail the tariff shift and origin would be South Korea under 102.11(b).
reasoning: The finished 4680 Cylindrical Can Assembly is classified in subheading 8507.90.8000. The good is neither wholly obtained (102.11(a)(1)) nor produced exclusively from domestic materials (102.11(a)(2)). Under 102.11(a)(3), the rule in 102.20(o) for subheading 8507.90 requires a change from any other subheading (with exceptions not applicable here). The Korean steel (Chapter 72), rivet (heading 7318/8308), and gasket (heading 3926/4016) are all classified outside 8507.90 and undergo the required tariff shift during production in Mexico.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the failing Chinese thermal module components (fins, heat pipes, vapor chamber, base, plate) classified in heading 8473
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the dedicated heat sink components (fins, heat pipes, vapor chamber, base) in China
